title: Serum creatinine elevation after renin-angiotensin system blockade and long term cardiorenal risks: cohort study
authors: Schmidt M, Mansfield KE, Bhaskaran K, Nitsch D, Sørensen HT, Smeeth L, et al.
followUp: 1997 to 2014; risks reported at 1, 5 and 10 years
population: Patients in UK primary care (Clinical Practice Research Datalink linked to Hospital Episode Statistics) starting an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, with creatinine measured within 12 months before and 2 months after the start, who continued treatment
funder: MS was supported by Aarhus University Hospital, the A.P. Møller Foundation for the Advancement of Medical Science, Snedkermester Sophus Jacobsen and Hustru Astrid Jacobsens Fond, and Christian og Ottilia Brorsons Rejselegat; HTS by the Program for Clinical Research Infrastructure established by the Lundbeck Foundation and the Novo Nordisk Foundation; KB by a Sir Henry Dale Fellowship jointly funded by the Wellcome Trust and the Royal Society; LAT and KEM by a Wellcome Trust intermediate clinical fellowship. None of these funding sources had a role in the design, conduct, analysis, or reporting of the study.
authorConflicts: The Department of Clinical Epidemiology, Aarhus, is involved in studies funded by various companies as research grants to Aarhus University, stated as unrelated to this study; no other relationships declared.
result: The authors attribute the creatinine rise after starting these drugs to antagonism of angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction, and cite data that only 10% of patients receive the recommended monitoring and only 20% of those with a rise of 30% or more discontinue. 2078 patients (1.7%) had a creatinine increase of 30% or more after starting treatment; they were more often women, aged 80 or over, with heart failure, and using non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, loop or potassium-sparing diuretics. Against increases below 30%, adjusted incidence rate ratios were 3.43 (95% CI 2.40 to 4.91) for end-stage renal disease, 1.46 (1.16 to 1.84) for myocardial infarction, 1.37 (1.14 to 1.65) for heart failure and 1.84 (1.65 to 2.05) for death; 10-year mortality was 49.2% against 22.5%. The relation was graded: against increases below 10%, increases of 10 to 19% gave a mortality rate ratio of 1.15 (1.09 to 1.22) and 20 to 29% gave 1.35 (1.23 to 1.49). The authors state that the 30% stopping threshold lacks a clear rationale, and that the results identify a high-risk group but do not necessarily support discontinuation.
